en: They say the argali’s flesh is finest;
In every way I shall exact blood-price
For Köksö, son of Aydarkan.
Meat tastes sweet when caught and eaten—
They say the gazelle’s flesh is finest;
I shall pursue and demand an accounting
For Köksö, son of Aydarkan.
When the teeming peoples gathered
At six-gated Beijing,
At the place from which none would retreat,
They settled the land and guarded Talas.
Driving on the man who said, ‘My horse is my only one,’
They slaughtered and ate his horse,
Driving him toward the Six Khans’ Beijing,
Driving him on, saying they would do battle.
When they reached the road midway,
And the great war drum was struck hard,
When the people clamored and spoke,
The man who said, ‘I alone am myself,’
Was driven on after they slaughtered and ate him,
Driven toward a deep-dug pit,
Driven toward a net in which he would be caught,
Driven toward torment where he would boil to death;
My noble father Köksö
Was led captive, tethered to a black horse.
His peerless steed was tied,
And all the giant champions
Were handed over to the forty warriors.
By force, there in Beijing,
He laid twelve khans to rest.
How could you have done this?
Heed what I am saying;
Without starting strife or raising turmoil,
Pay the blood-price for Köksö.
Lean, gray-maned Semetey,
If you are the hero Külchoro,
Then I am brave Ümötöy of Sary-Arka,
Whom no one has defeated in combat.
That is who I am.
If I bind tassels to my pinewood spear,
And demand the blood-price for Khan Köksö,
Accept the terms I have spoken.
Saying, ‘This is the price for your father Köksö;
This is your share of the blood-price,’
Give his son your answer.
Load gold coins and treasure
Upon Arbuurul.
Saying, ‘This is your father’s price,’
Bring before me the red roan with the sparse mane,
The fierce, slant-eyed steed,
Without suffering carnage or seeing strife;
Saying, ‘This is your father’s price,’
Lead it here before me.
With the roan horse at their head,
Quickly gather chosen horses from among the racers.
Without killing one another,
Gather them swiftly, causing no hardship.
Put your dark eyes up for sale;
Offer me Khan Bakay’s head as a gift!
Fold your hands and submit!
If you still know sin from merit,
Say, ‘We submit ourselves to you!’
My own cousin and dear friend,
Say, ‘We stand wholly at your command!’
This is all I now demand:
Pay my father’s blood-price now!
If I stiffen in anger
And my terrible rage takes hold,
Name the ridge beyond which you will cross;
There is no avoiding our confrontation—
Name the place where you will face me.
Name your pasture by twin Kara-Kyr.
If you will not heed my words,
If you will not pay my father’s price,
Name the place where we shall clash!
If you Kyrgyz say, ‘We will pay no blood-price,’
Do not smirk—speak the truth.
If you would meet us spear to spear,
If you would die exchanging gunfire,
If you would stand face-to-face,
Thrusting spears and firing bullets—
If you Kyrgyz are strong,
And would fight in bloody struggle,
I have no livestock I fear to leave strewn in the valley;
If you would fight to the death, Kyrgyz,
I have no life I wish to spare from death!
I have mustered an army for battle,
A vast host, leaving no man behind.
If I cannot take my father’s price,
Why should I remain at peace?
Valuing this life not even as a hair,
I shall fight to mutual destruction!
Through Achmaral, Merki, and broad Talas
I have come to carve a road;
Upon Semetey, the son of Manas,
I have come to launch an attack!
Yesterday, while that bloodthirsty leopard lived,
He stirred every conflict he knew;
Leaving not a single man behind,
He gathered hosts in their thousands.
Driving them onward to Kakan,
How many did he slaughter?
Had my father not gone,
Bound in humiliation and driven with the army,
Had he not gone there,
To conquer Beijing,
To bring calamity upon Beijing,
Rousing the nation and driving forth the host,
Driving such an immense army,
Humiliating some,
Pouring out his wrath and oppressing them,
Blunting their white-steel blades,
Leading all the giants and champions
Until they perished—
He began that dreadful tumult.
Driving all those mighty warriors
Deep into China,
He left them slaughtered there.
Agitated, seeking the spirit
Of my father who truly died,
Raging as I demand his blood-price,
I shall cry out and level my spear;
I shall slaughter many of you,
And stand against you in fury.
Our khans who deem themselves mighty,
Our many young and old—
Valuing our fleeting lives not even as a hair,
Today we shall all be slain!
Heed what has been said.
Do not quarrel or raise strife,
Do not fall into frantic confusion,
Do not cause an empty uproar
And fight like the Chinese.
Before the people are ruined and heroes die,
Before survivors can no longer endure life,
Heed these words:
Pay the blood-price of my father, Khan Köksö!
When he rode against teeming Beijing
With his spear leveled straight,
When the day was ending in a storm of bullets
And battle raged,
He found the suffering unbearable.
It was for this that my noble father
Entered the fray against Kakan,
And for this cause he died.
How would he ever have suffered such wrath
Had Khan Manas not unleashed his anger,
Had he not driven my father
To that Beijing?
How else would he have suffered such wrath?
When would my father, the khan and sovereign,
Have died, leaving his children orphans
And his wife a widow—
When else would my valiant father
Have died?
Heed these words of mine;
As recompense for that father,
Give me as much as I desire!
Without fighting or quarreling,
Without throwing the whole country into commotion,
Without throwing all the people into turmoil,
Heed what I have said;
Saying, ‘Such is the blood-price,’
Pay the price for my father the khan!
Give countless dark-brown camels,
And bales of robes of honor.
Upon the gelded camels
Load red gold and crimson silk,
Saying, ‘Take them without contention,’
As the price for my mighty father.
If Semetey will not fight,
Let him endure this great demand.
Let him give countless bald-faced mares;
Among all the mares he gives,
Let there be swift thoroughbreds—
Karabayyr horses with bronze-like legs,
Most of them chosen racers,
And let his finest runners be among them.
Let him make my father’s khanship
Known among the multitude.
Let the captured Surkoen
Not grow restless for nothing—
Let him be mounted by Changtiybes.
This is the point, this is my word:
Let him show that he will pay the blood-price!
Let them heed what has been said;
Without quarreling or raising strife,
Let them give whatever I desire.
If they will not agree to this,
If they will not give what I desire,
Let them stand face-to-face with us.
Firing muskets and drawing bows,
Let them fight us head-on.
I have come to witness
Their courage and lionheartedness;
My own cousin Semetey,
With slaves who will not retreat,
I have come to fight you to the death.
He has armor reaching from chest to shovel-length,
A coat that bullets cannot pierce.
If quarrel and conflict arise,
What a splendid chance for a warrior of slaughter!
Streaming out from Sary-Arka,
I have an army I drove here.”
So Ümötöy,
Pouring out his wrath and readying himself,
Prepared all his arms and armor
And stood there in fury.
Like one who would spare no life,
He committed this great outrage.
The smirking madman—
God had struck him senseless.
Then Külchoro,
Standing there, said this:
“Since I became Külchoro,
Since Külchoro first mounted a horse,
Since I grew to manhood as an orphan,
And somehow rejoined my people,
Since I came of age and became a hero,
The equal of heroic sons,
Since I donned the white invulnerable coat
And charged the foe with a battle cry,
Fate has not yet brought my death.
Among all round-headed mortals,
Ümötöy, son of Khan Köksö,
I have never seen a fool like you!
We drove white deer like cattle,
Made conquered lands our spoil,
And stirred conflict in barren lands;
Through the Six Cities and Margilan,
Down to Kokand and Samarkand,
Pursuing the blood-price of Chubak,
We sacked those very lands and won a hundredfold.
In Chinmachin and Kakan,
Did your father not see true warfare?
Your father Köksö
Fought a mighty battle,
And among the tribe called Soloon
Was raised up as khan.
He exercised sovereign power
And enjoyed his own khanship.
Far from being owed a blood-price, your father,
While still alive, exacted one himself,
Fulfilling all the desires
Of every fair-faced Kazakh,
And filling all his chests
With possessions of yellow gold.
Fulfilling every wish,
He filled every treasury
With an abundance of gold.
Exalting his khanship above the people,
Hiding his pastures beneath clouds of dust,
Driving humiliation away like sheep,
Hiding his enclosures beneath clouds of dust,
Raising his khanship above all others,
Your father conquered Beijing.
